kicker: Latent Sparse Attention, from the paper

scenes.text: A sparse attention layer reads only a few thousand keys. So why does it still crawl at ten million tokens?
scenes.say: A sparse attention layer reads only a few thousand keys per query. So why does it still crawl at ten million tokens?

scenes.headline: How LSA finds the keys without scoring them all
scenes.sub: Cluster the keys by meaning, then search the clusters
scenes.say: Hi, I'm Ladle! The answer is a hidden bill, and Latent Sparse Attention, or LSA, pays far less of it. Let's open it up.

scenes.title: The hidden bill
scenes.sub: Something has to choose which keys a query reads

steps.say: A new query could look at every earlier key. Sparse attention reads only a few thousand of them.

steps.term: Indexer: picks which keys a query reads
steps.say: Something has to choose those keys: the indexer. In production designs it still scores every earlier key, or every block of four.
Then attention runs on the chosen few. The attention got cheap. The choosing did not.

steps.note: linear per query, so quadratic over a prefill
steps.say: Scoring every key grows with the context, for every query. Over a whole prompt, that is quadratic again.

scenes.title: The indexer's share of the layer

steps.say: Here is the bill on GLM-5.3-Flash, measured by the paper on an H200. At half a million tokens, the indexer is two thirds of the layer.
Counting nothing but multiply-adds from the model configs lands in the same place.

steps.term: Prefill: reading the whole prompt in
steps.say: At ten million tokens, ninety-eight percent of prefill is spent choosing keys, not reading them. That is the shape of the algorithm, not a slow kernel.
The paper's own figure. Full attention in red, sparse in blue. Now look at the inset.
The light blue is the indexer. A free indexer would make this layer fifty-eight times faster again.

scenes.title: Buckets instead of keys
scenes.say: Chapter two. Buckets instead of keys.

scenes.text: Cluster the keys by meaning into buckets of about 8, and let each query score one centroid per bucket instead of every key.
scenes.say: Here's the idea. Cluster the keys by meaning into buckets of about eight. Then a query scores one centroid per bucket, instead of every key.

scenes.title: Buckets by meaning, one block at a time

legend: 512 keys in a block, 64 dims each
toy: a toy block: every key a point on a circle
Ward merges them, round by round

steps.say: Picture the index space in two dimensions: every key a point on a circle, its angle its meaning. A real block holds five hundred and twelve.
Every four neighbouring keys are summed into one pool key: a hundred and twenty-eight per block.

steps.term: Ward's method: merge what adds least scatter
steps.say: Ward's method merges them in rounds, always joining the pair that adds the least scatter, down to sixty-four buckets of about eight keys.
Each bucket keeps one centroid, its normalised key sum, and never changes again.
A query scores only the centroids, keeps the best buckets, and reads their keys.

scenes.title: One query, at a million tokens and beyond

steps.say: Now, one query at full scale. Its heads are summed into one index query, so one list serves every head.

steps.term: Centroid: a bucket's normalised key sum
steps.say: It scores every earlier centroid: one dot product per eight keys.
It keeps the best one thousand and twenty-four buckets.
It reads them best first, appending keys until it holds four thousand and ninety-six.
Add four sink keys and a five hundred and twelve key window: attention reads four thousand six hundred and twelve keys.
The paper draws the same path. Clustering happens once per block, here.
The top buckets expand into sink, long-range and window indices.
And on the right, a tree, for when scoring every bucket is too much.

scenes.title: At 10M, the tree searches the buckets

steps.term: Node bucket: four children, one centroid
steps.say: Flat scores every bucket, over a million at ten million tokens. The tree groups buckets into node buckets of four, and its beam starts at level three, scoring every node there.
It keeps the best two thousand and forty-eight, and scores only their children: eight thousand one hundred and ninety-two.
Keep two thousand and forty-eight again, and step down.
At the bucket level, it picks the top p from the last beam's children.
About forty-five thousand vectors scored, against one point three million for flat. Twenty-nine times fewer.

scenes.title: Does it hold up?
scenes.sub: The paper's speedups, and where they stop
scenes.say: Chapter three. Does it hold up?

steps.say: One layer at ten million tokens is seventy-two times faster than full attention. But a layer is not a model: end to end on Qwen, time to first token improves nine point two one times.
And the authors' own block-sparse baseline is faster end to end below a million tokens.
LSA pulls ahead only at ten million. It is a long-context method, and its own table says so.

scenes.title: Where it falls short
scenes.say: The article's own experiments, on synthetic keys, found the soft spots.

items.text: Pooling blurs keys that sit apart
items.say: Pooling assumes neighbours mean the same thing. On scattered keys at sixty-four k, recall fell to fifty-two point three percent, against ninety-nine point four without it.
Blocks of four, scoring twice as many vectors, beat shipped LSA almost everywhere.
And each level the tree's beam descends costs a little recall, with a beam already at the engine's limit.

scenes.text: Past a million tokens, choosing keys is the bill. LSA pays it once by clustering, so queries search buckets, not keys.
scenes.say: Past a million tokens, choosing keys is the bill. LSA pays it once, by clustering, so every query searches buckets instead of keys.

recap: The indexer is 98% of prefill at 10M
Ward buckets of about 8, one centroid each
Wins past 1M; pooling is the weak spot
scenes.say: To recap. At ten million tokens, the indexer is the bill. Buckets of about eight let a query score one centroid each. And it pays off past a million tokens.
